summary:
La Libertad stands under the national framework of Peru. Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. In February 2025 a congressional committee approved unanimously, for plenary debate, the dictamen of bills on bathroom access presented by Jorge Montoya of Honor y Democracia, restricting trans people's use of public bathrooms. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents then mandated that restroom entry be determined by biological sex, barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity, and the same package bans inclusive signage such as women in their diversity.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru found the bathroom provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity, implicitly framing them as harassment risks, and recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

The restriction reaches private and commercial life as well as state premises. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, and on television the presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to go use the men's room.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, alongside Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Two protective developments are on record nationally. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Speech and association are constrained as well. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Within La Libertad, lethal violence against LGBT people is concentrated. The Public Ministry's Observatory of Criminality study of intentional deaths of LGTB people in Peru covering 2012 to 2021 recorded 88 victims across 84 criminal complaints, and placed La Libertad second in absolute count with 10 victims, level with Lima Norte and behind Lima's 12. The region holds roughly 3% of the national population but accounted for about 11.4% of those deaths, a per-capita lethality of roughly 3.8 times the national average and a concentration not explained by population alone.

Six fiscal districts accounted for 58% of the deaths, namely Lima (12), La Libertad (10), Lima Norte (10), Lima Este (7), Lima Sur (6) and Callao (6), with 72 identified suspects. The study was developed with the Justice Ministry human-rights office and the University Cayetano Heredia LGTB-rights observatory with UNDP support, and yielded recommendations including training criminal prosecutors on LGTB-victim identification and monitoring systems.

Set against that record, Ordenanza Regional N.° 009-2024-GRLL-CR of the Regional Government of La Libertad, dated 6 September 2024, promotes labour inclusion of travesti, transsexual and transgender people in the region and recognises the trans community as a group in a situation of vulnerability there.
tangentialFactors:
La Libertad's standing in the national homicide ranking is comparative rather than unique: its 10 victims place it level with Lima Norte and behind Lima, and six fiscal districts together hold 58% of all recorded deaths. What distinguishes the region is the ratio between its population share and its share of the victims, which yields a per-capita lethality around 3.8 times the national average and pulls the unit's score below the national figure of 0.36.

The regional and national layers of governance in La Libertad move in opposite directions. The regional council adopted a positive-action measure for trans labour inclusion in September 2024, while the national Congress during the same period approved restrictions on bathroom access and removed LGBT hate-crime coverage from the Penal Code back in 2017. A visitor therefore encounters a protective instrument at the sub-national level that does not offset national statutory restrictions on facilities, and does not restore the hate-crime protection the national legislature repealed.

Public rhetoric continues to shape the environment in which the regional measure operates. The Inter-American Court's Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 and IDEHPUCP's critique of the bathroom provision supply an international and academic counterweight to the congressional position, while public figures such as Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV and congressman Lizarzaburu have made statements directed at LGBT people on national stages.

Enforcement of the national facilities policy has already reached private premises far from the capital: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that applied it. Sentencing in the Azul Rojas Marín case in December 2025 shows that litigation through the Inter-American Commission and the Inter-American Court can deliver a conviction, but the case took close to twenty years.
localsOnly:
Ordenanza Regional N.° 000009-2024-GRLL-CR was presented in the Regional Council of La Libertad's ordinary session of 3 September 2024, debated, approved and signed in Trujillo on 6 September 2024, and published in El Peruano on 7 November 2024, entering into force the day after publication.

The ordinance's object is positive-action measures for the effective labour inclusion of travesti, transsexual and transgender persons in La Libertad, securing their right to formal, dignified and productive work in equitable and satisfactory conditions without discrimination on grounds of gender identity or its expression. It cites constitutional equality guarantees and article 323 of the Penal Code, under which discrimination is a crime, and recalls a 2014 regional-council session framework against discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity.

The ordinance recommends that local governments issue municipal ordinances recognising gender identity and fundamental rights, and orders the establishment of a working group (mesa de trabajo) to carry its measures out. Residents of La Libertad are the beneficiaries of the recognition of the trans community as a group in a situation of vulnerability in the region.

Nationally, residents also benefit from the June 2024 removal of pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, and from the July 2025 ruling of a Lima constitutional court, obtained after an activist legal challenge, that an anti-equality decree was unconstitutional.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Public Ministry study counts deaths of LGTB people as a category and does not disaggregate transgender or gender-diverse victims. No figure for trans-specific homicide in La Libertad, as distinct from LGBT homicide generally, is available in the sourced material, and the 2012-2021 window means the tally does not cover the period in which the national bathroom restrictions were adopted.

Whether the April 2025 bathroom mandate has been applied to public premises in Trujillo or elsewhere in La Libertad, and how regional authorities have responded to it, is not sourced. Enforcement data for the region is limited to a single national-level instance, the gym complaint dismissed by a consumer-protection body.

Implementation of Ordenanza Regional N.° 009-2024-GRLL-CR is unresolved: the sourced material records the mandate to convene a working group and the recommendation that municipalities adopt their own ordinances, but no record of the working group's composition or output, and no municipal ordinance adopted under the recommendation. The origin and current status of the petition claiming one million signatures cited during the 2017 Penal Code repeal is not sourced beyond its mention in the congressional vote.
